chapter: The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Cortex
vignette: A 62-year-old right-handed woman presents with sudden cognitive difficulty. On examination, language fluency and auditory comprehension are intact. However, she is unable to perform simple calculations like 7 + 5 (acalculia), cannot write a simple sentence despite normal motor hand strength (agraphia), cannot tell her left hand from her right hand (right-left disorientation), and cannot distinguish or name individual fingers when touched (finger agnosia). Primary sensory modalities are intact.
question: Which cortical region is infarcted to produce Gerstmann syndrome?
options: Right (non-dominant) inferior parietal lobule
Left supramarginal gyrus and arcuate fasciculus
Left inferior frontal gyrus (Broca area)
Left (dominant) angular gyrus of the inferior parietal lobule
Left superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke area)

explanation.why_correct: The tetrad of: (1) agraphia without alexia, (2) acalculia, (3) finger agnosia, and (4) right-left disorientation constitutes classic Gerstmann syndrome. It localizes precisely to the dominant (usually left) angular gyrus of the inferior parietal lobule (Brodmann area 39), which serves as a major multimodal integration zone for language, spatial representation of the body schema, and arithmetic symbols.
distractors: Non-dominant (right) parietal lesions produce hemispatial neglect, anosognosia, constructional apraxia, and dressing apraxia.
Supramarginal gyrus and arcuate fasciculus lesions produce conduction aphasia (impaired repetition with intact comprehension).
Broca area (inferior frontal gyrus) lesions produce non-fluent expressive motor aphasia.
Wernicke area (superior temporal gyrus) lesions produce fluent sensory aphasia with impaired comprehension and neologisms.
explanation.key_point: Gerstmann syndrome (acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, right-left disorientation) localizes to the dominant (left) angular gyrus of the inferior parietal lobule.

chapter: The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Cortex
vignette: A 68-year-old man suffers cardiac arrest with severe hypotension. After resuscitation, his visual acuity is 20/20, but he cannot reach out and grab a pen held in front of him (reaching wildly off to the side). When shown a picture of a busy street scene, he can describe individual details (such as a red car) but cannot perceive or comprehend the scene as a unified whole. He is also unable to voluntarily direct his gaze toward new visual targets, although involuntary ocular pursuit is normal.
question: What is the diagnosis and anatomic localization of Bálint syndrome?
options: Unilateral dominant parietal lobe infarction with visual agnosia
Bilateral occipital calcarine infarctions (Anton syndrome)
Bilateral watershed parieto-occipital infarctions (Bálint syndrome: optic ataxia, simultanagnosia, and psychic paralysis of gaze)
Frontal eye field bilateral infarctions
Corpus callosum anterior trunk infarction

explanation.why_correct: Bálint syndrome is the classic clinical triad of: (1) optic ataxia (inability to guide the hand to reach an object under visual guidance despite normal limb strength), (2) simultanagnosia (inability to perceive more than one visual item at a time or integrate parts into a whole), and (3) ocular apraxia / psychic paralysis of gaze (inability to voluntarily redirect gaze to a new visual target). It is caused by bilateral damage to the dorsal visual stream in the parieto-occipital junctions, classically occurring after watershed borderzone infarction between the MCA and PCA following severe systemic hypotension.
distractors: Unilateral parietal lesions cause hemispatial neglect or Gerstmann syndrome, not the full triad of Bálint syndrome.
Anton syndrome is cortical blindness with visual anosognosia (denial of blindness), caused by bilateral calcarine striate cortex infarctions.
Frontal eye field lesions cause gaze deviation toward the lesion acutely, but do not produce simultanagnosia or optic ataxia.
Corpus callosum lesions cause split-brain disconnection syndromes (callosal apraxia, alien hand syndrome).
explanation.key_point: Bálint syndrome consists of optic ataxia, simultanagnosia, and ocular apraxia, localizing to bilateral parieto-occipital borderzone lesions.

vignette: A 58-year-old right-handed man presents with a sudden speech abnormality after a cardioembolic stroke. During testing, his spontaneous speech is fluent and effortless, though peppered with phonemic paraphasias (e.g., saying 'plip' for 'clip'). His auditory comprehension is remarkably intact, and he readily obeys complex multi-step commands. However, when asked to repeat the simple phrase 'No ifs, ands, or buts', he is completely unable to do so, repeatedly stumbling and producing distorted phonemes.
question: Which white matter tract / cortical region disconnection classically characterizes conduction aphasia?
options: Corpus callosum anterior forceps connecting bilateral frontal lobes
Arcuate fasciculus / superior longitudinal fasciculus connecting Wernicke and Broca areas
Uncinate fasciculus connecting amygdala to orbitofrontal cortex
Inferior longitudinal fasciculus connecting occipital to temporal cortex
Anterior commissure connecting bilateral middle temporal gyri

explanation.why_correct: Conduction aphasia is classical disconnective aphasia characterized by: (1) FLUENT spontaneous speech with prominent phonemic paraphasias, (2) INTACT auditory comprehension, and (3) DISPROPORTIONATELY SEVERE impairment in repetition. It is caused by lesions in the arcuate fasciculus (or supramarginal gyrus / auditory-motor interface area Spt) in the dominant parietal/temporal operculum, disconnecting Wernicke area (auditory comprehension) from Broca area (motor articulation).
distractors: The anterior forceps connects bilateral prefrontal cortices; its disruption does not cause isolated severe repetition failure.
The uncinate fasciculus connects the anterior temporal lobe with the orbitofrontal cortex (social behavior and naming), not repetition.
The inferior longitudinal fasciculus connects visual cortex to anterior temporal lobe (visual object recognition).
The anterior commissure mediates interhemispheric transfer of temporal and olfactory information.
explanation.key_point: Conduction aphasia = fluent speech + intact comprehension + severely impaired repetition, localized to the arcuate fasciculus or supramarginal gyrus.

vignette: A 62-year-old right-handed woman is evaluated following an ischemic stroke. On cognitive testing, she cannot perform simple subtraction or addition (acalculia), cannot write sentences or her name despite normal hand motor power (agraphia), cannot identify or distinguish between the fingers on her own hand or the examiner's hand (finger agnosia), and confuses her right hand with her left hand (right-left disorientation). Her speech is fluent and comprehension is intact.
question: Which cortical region of the dominant (left) hemisphere is damaged in Gerstmann syndrome?
options: Left angular gyrus (Brodmann area 39) in the inferior parietal lobule
Left Broca area (Brodmann area 44/45) in the inferior frontal gyrus
Left Wernicke area (Brodmann area 22) in the superior temporal gyrus
Right supramarginal gyrus (Brodmann area 40)
Left fusiform gyrus (Brodmann area 37)

explanation.why_correct: Gerstmann syndrome is a classic tetrad consisting of: (1) Agraphia without alexia, (2) Acalculia (loss of arithmetic capacity), (3) Finger agnosia (inability to recognize, name, or select individual fingers), and (4) Right-left disorientation. This tetrad localizes precisely to a lesion in the dominant (usually left) angular gyrus (Brodmann area 39) in the inferior parietal lobule, or subcortical white matter immediately beneath it, supplied by the angular branch of the middle cerebral artery.
distractors: Broca area lesions cause expressive nonfluent aphasia, not isolated Gerstmann tetrad.
Wernicke area lesions cause receptive fluent aphasia with impaired comprehension, not preserved comprehension.
Right parietal lesions cause left hemispatial neglect, anosognosia, and constructional apraxia.
Fusiform gyrus lesions cause prosopagnosia (inability to recognize familiar faces), not acalculia and finger agnosia.
explanation.key_point: Gerstmann syndrome (acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, right-left disorientation) localizes to the dominant (left) angular gyrus (Brodmann area 39).

source_quote: the dominant medial occipital region (particularly lesions involving the cortex around and below the calcarine fissure) and the inferior fibers of the splenium
vignette: A 66-year-old retired schoolteacher experiences an acute left posterior cerebral artery stroke. When given a pen, he can fluently write a detailed paragraph describing his symptoms. However, a minute later, when asked to read the very paragraph he just wrote, he is completely unable to read it ('I cannot read the words, though I know I wrote them'). Visual field testing shows a complete right homonymous hemianopia.
question: What two anatomical structures are infarcted/disconnected to produce alexia without agraphia (pure alexia)?
options: Left angular gyrus and the anterior corpus callosum
Bilateral frontal eye fields and the genu of the internal capsule
Left Broca area and the optic chiasm
Left primary visual cortex (calcarine cortex) and the splenium of the corpus callosum
Left superior temporal gyrus and the arcuate fasciculus

explanation.why_correct: Alexia without agraphia (pure alexia or Dejerine alexia) is the archetypal cerebral disconnection syndrome. It requires two components: (1) Infarction of the left primary visual cortex (producing a right homonymous hemianopia); and (2) Infarction of the splenium of the corpus callosum (which normally carries visual information from the intact right visual cortex across to the language centers in the left hemisphere). Visual input received by the intact right hemisphere cannot reach the left angular gyrus for reading decoding; however, writing is preserved because the left angular gyrus and Broca area remain intact.
distractors: A lesion of the left angular gyrus causes alexia WITH agraphia, destroying both reading and writing.
Frontal eye fields control voluntary saccades, not reading comprehension.
Broca area does not cause pure alexia and optic chiasm produces bitemporal hemianopia.
Arcuate fasciculus lesions produce conduction aphasia, not pure alexia.
explanation.key_point: Alexia without agraphia results from combined infarction of the left visual cortex and splenium of the corpus callosum (left PCA occlusion).

vignette: A 59-year-old woman suffers severe systemic hypotension during coronary artery bypass surgery. Postoperatively, she has profound visual difficulty despite 20/20 visual acuity. When shown a pen and asked to grab it, her hand erratically misses the pen entirely (optic ataxia). When shown a picture containing a comb, a spoon, and a coin, she can see only the spoon and is completely blind to the other objects in the scene (simultanagnosia). She cannot voluntarily direct her gaze toward objects presented in her visual periphery (ocular apraxia / psychic paralysis of gaze).
question: What is the eponym for this triad (optic ataxia, simultanagnosia, ocular apraxia), and where is the anatomical lesion located?
options: Anton syndrome due to bilateral striate cortex infarctions
Bálint syndrome due to bilateral watershed infarctions of the parieto-occipital association cortices
Capgras syndrome due to bifrontal contusions
Charles Bonnet syndrome due to peripheral macular degeneration
Klüver-Bucy syndrome due to bilateral anterior temporal lobectomies

explanation.why_correct: Bálint syndrome is the classic triad of: (1) Simultanagnosia (inability to perceive more than one object at a time or comprehend a visual scene as a whole); (2) Optic ataxia (impaired visually guided reaching in the absence of primary motor or cerebellar deficit); and (3) Ocular apraxia / psychic paralysis of gaze (inability to initiate voluntary saccades to visual targets). It is caused by bilateral infarctions of the posterior parietal and parieto-occipital cortices (Brodmann areas 7 and 19), typically resulting from watershed/borderzone hypoperfusion between the MCA and PCA territories after severe hypotension.
distractors: Anton syndrome is visual anosognosia (cortical blindness where the patient denies being blind and confabulates visual experiences) due to bilateral calcarine cortex destruction.
Capgras delusion is the belief that familiar persons have been replaced by identical impostors.
Charles Bonnet syndrome refers to vivid, formed visual hallucinations occurring in mentally intact individuals with severe peripheral visual loss.
Klüver-Bucy syndrome involves hyperorality, hypersexuality, and psychic blindness from bilateral amygdala/anterior temporal lesions.
explanation.key_point: Bálint syndrome (simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, ocular apraxia) is caused by bilateral parieto-occipital watershed infarctions (MCA-PCA boundary zone).

source_quote: the nondominant hemisphere mediates attentional mechanisms directed to both hemifields, whereas the left hemisphere is concerned mainly with the right hemispace
vignette: A 72-year-old man suffers an acute ischemic stroke of the right cerebral hemisphere. On examination, he lies in bed with his head and eyes turned to the right. When asked to draw a clock face, he crowds all the numbers 1 through 12 onto the right half of the circle and completely ignores the left half. When the examiner touches both of the patient's hands simultaneously, he perceives touch only on the right hand (sensory extinction to double simultaneous stimulation), despite perceiving left touch normally when tested alone.
question: Which cortical region is most critical for directing bilateral spatial attention, whose unilateral lesion produces severe hemispatial neglect?
options: Left precentral motor cortex of the dominant hemisphere
Bilateral medial occipital lobes (cuneus and lingual gyri)
Right inferior parietal lobule (temporoparietal junction) of the non-dominant hemisphere
Right gyrus rectus in the orbitofrontal cortex
Left superior temporal pole

explanation.why_correct: The right (nondominant) hemisphere—particularly the right inferior parietal lobule and temporoparietal junction (Brodmann area 39/40)—plays a dominant, asymmetric role in directing spatial attention across BOTH the right and left visual hemispaces. The left hemisphere directs attention almost exclusively to the contralateral right hemispace. Therefore, a right hemispheric lesion leaves only the left hemisphere operating, creating dense, profound neglect of the left hemispace (anosognosia, left hemineglect, clock drawing error, sensory extinction). A left hemispheric lesion rarely causes severe neglect because the intact right hemisphere attends to both sides.
distractors: Left precentral motor cortex produces contralateral right hemiplegia without left-sided neglect.
Bilateral medial occipital lesions cause cortical blindness or lower visual field cuts.
The gyrus rectus is involved in olfaction and emotional regulation, not visuospatial attention.
The left superior temporal pole mediates auditory memory and semantic processing.
explanation.key_point: Right inferior parietal lobule / temporoparietal junction lesions produce contralateral hemispatial neglect because the right hemisphere uniquely attends to both hemispaces.

vignette: A 65-year-old man suffers an acute destructive ischemic stroke of the right frontal lobe involving Brodmann area 8. On examination, his eyes are conjugate and deviated to the right ('looking toward the lesion'). He cannot voluntarily look to the left. However, when the examiner briskly turns the patient's head to the right, his eyes reflexively deviate smoothly and fully across to the left (positive oculocephalic reflex).
question: What neuroanatomical pathway does the frontal eye field (FEF) drive to produce horizontal saccades, and why did the doll's eye maneuver succeed?
options: FEF drives the ipsilateral abducens nucleus directly; the reflex activates the cerebellum

FEF drives the CONTRALATERAL pontine paramedian reticular formation (PPRF) via crossed descending corticopontine pathways; the oculocephalic reflex uses an intact brainstem VOR circuit that bypasses the cortex
FEF projects to the spinal accessory nucleus to turn the head first; the reflex acts through the cervical cord
FEF controls only vertical saccades; the horizontal deviation was purely an epileptic focus
FEF innervates the medial rectus directly without brainstem relays

explanation.why_correct: The frontal eye field (FEF, Brodmann area 8) initiates voluntary, fast horizontal saccades to the CONTRALATERAL side by sending descending fibers that decussate at the pontine level to activate the contralateral paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) and CN VI nucleus. An acute destructive right FEF lesion leaves the left FEF unopposed, driving gaze tonically to the RIGHT ('the patient looks toward the destructive hemispheric lesion'). The preserved oculocephalic reflex (doll's eyes) proves that the lower pontine machinery (PPRF, CN VI, MLF, CN III) is fully intact and activated directly by vestibular labyrinthine afferents.
distractors: FEF projects to the CONTRALATERAL PPRF, not ipsilateral CN VI directly.
Head turning is driven by SCM, but conjugate saccades are driven by PPRF relays.
FEF coordinates horizontal saccades; vertical saccades are coordinated in the midbrain (riMLF).
FEF does not project monosynaptically to the medial rectus; it requires PPRF and MLF relays.
explanation.key_point: A destructive frontal eye field lesion causes conjugate gaze deviation toward the lesion; preserved oculocephalic reflex confirms the pontine gaze center is intact.

chapter: The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Cortex
source_quote: centered in the posterior two-thirds of the superior temporal gyrus affecting the auditory association cortex (area 22 of Brodmann, or Wernicke's area)
vignette: A 67-year-old right-handed man is brought in by his wife after sudden speech difficulty. His speech is effortless, melodic and fluent, but is full of wrong or invented words and is largely unintelligible. He cannot follow simple spoken commands, cannot repeat a sentence and cannot name objects. He has no hemiparesis or sensory loss and appears anxious and agitated.
question: Which lesion best explains this language disorder?
options: Left posterior inferior frontal gyrus (Broca area)
Left temporal pole (area 38)
Left supramarginal gyrus (area 40) alone
Right posterior temporoparietal region
Posterior two-thirds of the left superior temporal gyrus

explanation.why_correct: Fluent, well-articulated but paraphasic speech with severely impaired auditory comprehension, repetition and naming is Wernicke aphasia. It follows infarction centered in the posterior superior temporal gyrus (auditory association cortex, area 22). Hemiparesis and sensory loss are often absent or mild, so these patients may be mistaken for psychiatric cases.
distractors: Broca area lesions produce effortful, nonfluent, agrammatic speech with preserved comprehension, the opposite of this patient's profile.
Damage to the left anterior temporal cortex (area 38 and neighboring areas) causes a pure naming defect (especially for proper nouns) without comprehension or phonemic problems.
A discrete supramarginal gyrus infarct causes conduction aphasia, in which comprehension is good enough to hold a normal conversation and repetition is the main deficit.
Right posterior temporoparietal lesions impair the perception of emotional overtones of speech (sensory aprosodia), not the comprehension of words.
explanation.key_point: Wernicke aphasia (fluent, paraphasic, poor comprehension and repetition) localizes to the posterior superior temporal gyrus (area 22) of the dominant hemisphere.

chapter: The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Cortex
source_quote: there is a mild and transient aphasia referred to as Broca area aphasia
vignette: A 58-year-old right-handed woman has a small embolic infarct that MRI shows is confined to the posterior part of the left inferior frontal gyrus and its subjacent white matter. The surrounding premotor cortex, the frontoparietal operculum, the supramarginal gyrus and the temporal lobe are spared. On day 1 her speech is sparse and lacks spontaneity.
question: Which course is expected for her language disturbance?
options: Lasting severe aphasia with agrammatic, telegraphic speech and markedly reduced fluency
A mild, transient aphasia that clears within days to weeks
Permanent fluent aphasia with poor comprehension and repetition
Global aphasia with right hemiplegia
Pure word deafness

explanation.why_correct: When damage is restricted to Broca area or its subjacent white matter, true Broca aphasia does not develop. Instead there is a mild, transient aphasia with decreased spontaneity that clears completely within days or weeks.
distractors: Lasting Broca aphasia with pronounced agrammatism requires larger lesions that extend across the frontoparietal operculum (including the postcentral and supramarginal gyri) and Wernicke area, or surrounding frontal fields and white matter.
A permanent fluent aphasia with poor comprehension is the picture of posterior (Wernicke) lesions, which are spared here.
Global aphasia with hemiplegia follows large perisylvian infarcts in the middle cerebral artery territory, not a small focal lesion.
Pure word deafness results from bilateral temporal cortical (or subcortical) lesions and is not produced by a left frontal lesion.
explanation.key_point: A lesion limited to Broca area causes only a mild, transient aphasia; lasting Broca aphasia needs a larger lesion of the surrounding frontal and perisylvian regions.

chapter: The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Cortex
source_quote: Pure word deafness results from bilateral temporal cortical lesions
vignette: A 64-year-old man had a left temporal stroke two years ago with full recovery and now has a new right temporal cortical infarct. Audiometry shows adequate hearing, yet he says people sound as if they speak a foreign language and he cannot understand speech. He reads, writes and speaks normally, though loudly, and understands better when he watches the speaker's lips.
question: Which lesion pattern best explains this disorder?
options: Isolated left posterior superior temporal gyrus lesion (Wernicke area)
Bilateral temporal cortical lesions involving the auditory cortices
Left posterior inferior frontal gyrus lesion (Broca area)
Right posterior temporoparietal lesion
Bilateral occipitotemporal lesions

explanation.why_correct: Inability to identify spoken words despite normal hearing, with preserved reading, writing and speech, is pure word deafness. It results from bilateral temporal cortical lesions, or from bilateral subcortical lesions that isolate the primary auditory cortex from its input. Patients improve with lip reading, not with louder sound.
distractors: A unilateral Wernicke area lesion produces fluent aphasia with impaired reading comprehension and paraphasic speech, not preserved reading and speaking.
Broca area lesions affect speech production, not the recognition of spoken words.
Right posterior temporoparietal lesions cause sensory aprosodia (poor perception of the emotional tone of speech), not loss of word recognition.
Bilateral occipitotemporal lesions cause visual problems such as agnosias, prosopagnosia or achromatopsia, not a failure to understand spoken words.
explanation.key_point: Pure word deafness: normal hearing and normal reading, writing and speech, caused by bilateral temporal cortical (or subcortical) lesions.

chapter: The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Cortex
source_quote: Patients with acute, bilateral, and extensive medial occipital lesions that render them blind may deny having any difficulty with seeing
vignette: A 71-year-old woman has sudden bilateral loss of vision after cardiac surgery. Pupillary light reflexes are normal. She walks into furniture but insists she can see well and describes in detail the clothes of the examiner, which she cannot possibly be seeing. She is also confabulating about recent events.
question: Which lesion pattern is most likely?
options: Bilateral parietooccipital convexity lesions
Acute, extensive bilateral medial occipital lesions, extending into visual association cortex
Bilateral inferior occipitotemporal lesions (lingual and fusiform gyri) sparing the calcarine cortex
Right inferior parietal lobule lesion
Bilateral anterior temporal lobe lesions

explanation.why_correct: Cortical blindness with denial of the deficit and confabulation about what is seen is Anton syndrome (visual anosognosia). It occurs with acute, bilateral, extensive medial occipital lesions, and discrete lesions tend to extend beyond the calcarine cortex into areas 18 and 19. Normal pupillary reflexes fit a cortical rather than anterior visual pathway cause.
distractors: Bilateral parietooccipital convexity lesions cause visual simultanagnosia and the Balint syndrome, in which acuity is preserved and the patient does not deny blindness.
Lingual and fusiform lesions sparing the calcarine cortex cause cerebral achromatopsia (loss of color perception), not blindness.
A right inferior parietal lesion causes left hemispatial neglect and anosognosia for hemiparesis, not bilateral blindness.
Bilateral anterior temporal lesions cause a bland affect and naming or semantic problems, not blindness.
explanation.key_point: Anton syndrome is blindness with denial of blindness from acute bilateral medial occipital lesions (often extending to areas 18 and 19).

chapter: The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Cortex
source_quote: In most postmortem examinations of patients with prosopagnosia, both fusiform gyri have been destroyed or disconnected
vignette: A 60-year-old man with bilateral posterior cerebral artery occlusions has normal visual acuity and fields. He cannot recognize his wife or children by sight but identifies them immediately when they speak. He can describe individual facial features, and when he looks in a mirror he reports seeing nothing familiar.
question: Which structures are most characteristically damaged?
options: Both fusiform gyri (inferior occipitotemporal cortex)
Bilateral parietooccipital convexities
Left medial occipital cortex and splenium of the corpus callosum
Bilateral superior temporal gyri
Left angular gyrus

explanation.why_correct: Inability to recognize familiar faces (even one's own) with preserved perception of facial features and recognition by voice is prosopagnosia. In most postmortem studies both fusiform gyri were destroyed or disconnected, so the fusiform gyrus functions as the visual association area for face recognition. Bilateral inferior occipitotemporal lesions, typically from bilateral PCA occlusion, produce it.
distractors: Bilateral parietooccipital lesions produce visual simultanagnosia and the Balint syndrome, in which the whole of a scene cannot be perceived.
Left medial occipital cortex plus splenium causes alexia without agraphia, a reading disorder.
Bilateral superior temporal lesions cause word deafness or auditory agnosia, not visual recognition failure.
A left angular gyrus lesion causes alexia with agraphia and components of Gerstmann syndrome, not loss of face recognition.
explanation.key_point: Prosopagnosia usually follows bilateral fusiform (inferior occipitotemporal) lesions, as in bilateral PCA occlusion.

chapter: The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Cortex
source_quote: Acquired achromatopsia appears with bilateral or nondominant inferior occipitotemporal lesions that damage the lingual and fusiform gyri
vignette: A 55-year-old man with vertebrobasilar disease has sudden loss of color vision. Visual acuity is normal, but he cannot read Ishihara plates or sort colored objects by hue, and he describes the world as gray. Perimetry shows bilateral superior quadrantanopia.
question: Which vascular and anatomic pattern explains his deficit?
options: Left inferomesial occipitotemporal and subsplenial lesion with right hemianopia
Bilateral calcarine cortex infarction
Bilateral inferior occipitotemporal lesions damaging the lingual and fusiform gyri, with the calcarine cortex spared
Bilateral parietooccipital watershed infarction

explanation.why_correct: Inability to read Ishihara plates or sort by hue is cortical color blindness (achromatopsia). It appears with bilateral or nondominant inferior occipitotemporal lesions of the lingual and fusiform gyri, sparing the calcarine cortex; the vascular lesion involves the inferior occipital branch of the PCA while sparing its calcarine branch. Associated superior quadrantanopia is common.
distractors: A dominant left inferomesial lesion with right hemianopia and pure alexia causes color agnosia, in which patients can read Ishihara plates and sort hues but cannot name colors.
Bilateral calcarine destruction causes cortical blindness, not an isolated loss of color perception.
Bilateral parietooccipital watershed lesions cause the Balint syndrome, not selective loss of color.
explanation.key_point: Achromatopsia (cannot sort or read colors) = bilateral or nondominant lingual and fusiform lesions sparing calcarine cortex; color agnosia (cannot name colors) = dominant inferomesial lesion.

chapter: The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Cortex
source_quote: Name objects, kept from view, palpated by the left hand (unilateral tactile anomia)
vignette: A 34-year-old right-handed man underwent section of the corpus callosum and anterior commissure for intractable epilepsy. Afterwards he has normal strength and sensation in both hands. Blindfolded, he cannot name an object placed in his left hand, although he names objects in his right hand without difficulty. He also cannot write with his left hand.
question: What best explains the left-hand deficits?
options: Left angular gyrus infarction
Right postcentral gyrus lesion causing astereognosis
Left Broca area lesion
Bilateral thalamic lesions
Disconnection of the right hemisphere from the language-dominant left hemisphere

explanation.why_correct: After callosal section, the left hand and its sensory information are controlled by the right hemisphere, which cannot transmit to the language-dominant left hemisphere. This produces unilateral tactile anomia and unilateral agraphia of the left hand, with normal naming for the right hand. Deficits often become apparent only on specific testing.
distractors: A left angular gyrus lesion would impair reading and writing with both hands (alexia with agraphia) and would not spare the right hand.
A right postcentral lesion would impair discrimination of shape and size in the left hand (astereognosis), but the patient here has normal sensation and cannot even write with the left hand.
A Broca area lesion would impair speech production for both hands and cause nonfluent speech.
Bilateral thalamic lesions cause memory and attention problems or sensory loss, not a hemisphere-specific naming failure.
explanation.key_point: Callosal disconnection in a left-dominant person causes left-hand tactile anomia, left-hand agraphia and left-sided apraxia without primary sensory or motor loss.

chapter: The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Cortex
source_quote: Lesions of this area lead to disinhibition and changes of affect. Behavior is impulsive (pseudopsychopathic)
vignette: A 45-year-old man sustains bilateral frontal base contusions in a motor vehicle accident. He is fully oriented and scores normally on a standard cognitive battery. However, he makes inappropriate jokes, is impulsive, is emotionally labile, and shows poor judgment about social situations.
question: Which region is most likely damaged?
options: Bilateral orbitofrontal and ventromedial prefrontal cortex
Bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal convexities
Bilateral medial frontal cortex (supplementary motor area and anterior cingulate)
Bilateral anterior temporal lobes

explanation.why_correct: Disinhibition, impulsivity (pseudopsychopathic behavior), inappropriate jocular affect (witzelsucht), emotional lability and poor judgment, with normal scores on ordinary cognitive tests, characterize the orbitofrontal and ventromedial prefrontal syndrome. These lesions are usually bilateral.
distractors: Large bilateral lesions of the prefrontal convexity cause apathy, indifference, psychomotor retardation and poor planning, not disinhibition.
Medial frontal lesions cause an akinetic syndrome, with paucity of spontaneous movement and speech, and akinetic mutism when large and bilateral.
Bilateral anterior temporal lesions cause a bland affect rather than impulsivity.
explanation.key_point: Orbitofrontal/ventromedial lesions give a disinhibited, pseudopsychopathic syndrome with preserved scores on cognitive testing.

chapter: The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Cortex
source_quote: results from damage to the supplementary motor area, anterior cingulate gyrus, and medial prefrontal cortex of the dominant hemisphere and anterior corpus callosum
vignette: A 63-year-old right-handed man has an acute stroke. In the following days his right hand repeatedly grasps objects placed near it, gropes toward the examiner, and compulsively manipulates tools, all against his will. The palm grasp reflex is present on the right, and he has no aphasia.
question: Which lesion best explains this picture?
options: Right inferior parietal lobule
Left angular gyrus
Splenium of the corpus callosum with left medial occipital cortex
Dominant medial frontal region: supplementary motor area, anterior cingulate and medial prefrontal cortex, with anterior corpus callosum
Left Broca area

explanation.why_correct: Reflexive grasping, groping and compulsive manipulation of tools in the dominant hand define the frontal alien hand syndrome. It results from damage to the supplementary motor area, anterior cingulate gyrus and medial prefrontal cortex of the dominant hemisphere and the anterior corpus callosum, producing a release of exploratory reflexes.
distractors: A right inferior parietal lesion causes left hemispatial neglect and anosognosia, not purposeless grasping of the right hand.
A left angular gyrus lesion causes alexia with agraphia and parts of Gerstmann syndrome, not compulsive tool manipulation.
Left medial occipital plus splenial lesions cause alexia without agraphia, a disconnection reading disorder, not a motor release phenomenon.
A Broca area lesion causes nonfluent aphasia; the hand symptoms and grasp reflex here point to the medial frontal region.
explanation.key_point: The frontal alien hand (dominant hand, grasping, groping, tool manipulation) follows dominant SMA, anterior cingulate and medial prefrontal damage plus anterior callosum.

chapter: The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Cortex
source_quote: All patients have an inferior-anterior parietal stroke involving the parietal operculum and posterior insula
vignette: A 59-year-old woman has sudden right-sided loss of touch, pain, temperature and vibration sense involving the face, arm and leg together. She has no significant weakness. MRI shows an acute cortical infarct but no thalamic lesion. Weeks later she develops a central neuropathic pain syndrome.
question: Where is the infarct most likely located?
options: Superior-posterior parietal cortex
Left angular gyrus
Paracentral lobule
Left parietal operculum and posterior insula

explanation.why_correct: A faciobrachiocrural loss of elementary sensation (touch, pain, temperature, vibration) from a cortical stroke without thalamic involvement is the pseudothalamic sensory syndrome. All such patients have an inferior-anterior parietal stroke involving the parietal operculum and posterior insula (S3, receiving spinothalamic projections), and about half develop central neuropathic pain.
distractors: A superior-posterior parietal stroke produces the cortical sensory syndrome, with loss of discriminative sensation (stereognosis, graphesthesia, position sense) in one or two body parts, not loss of pain and temperature.
A left angular gyrus lesion causes alexia with agraphia and Gerstmann components, not hemisensory loss to all modalities.
The paracentral lobule is a medial frontal-parietal area whose lesions give leg weakness and sensory loss mainly in the leg, not face, arm and leg together.
explanation.key_point: Pseudothalamic sensory syndrome (all-modality faciobrachiocrural loss, later neuropathic pain) = parietal operculum plus posterior insula.

chapter: The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Cortex
source_quote: Smaller lesions that destroy only a discrete portion of the cortex, such as infarcts, circumscribed to the supramarginal gyrus (area 40)
vignette: A 52-year-old right-handed woman has a small embolic infarct of the left hemisphere. Her speech is fluent and understandable, with frequent phonemic paraphasias. She comprehends conversation and complex commands normally but cannot repeat sentences she has just understood. Writing and naming are only mildly affected.
question: Which discrete cortical lesion best explains the profile?
options: Posterior two-thirds of the left superior temporal gyrus
Left posterior inferior frontal gyrus
Left angular gyrus
Posterior left middle temporal gyrus (area 37)
Left supramarginal gyrus (area 40)

explanation.why_correct: Fluent speech with good comprehension but impaired repetition and paraphasic errors is conduction aphasia. Small cortical infarcts circumscribed to the supramarginal gyrus (area 40) or the auditory cortex (areas 41, 42 and part of 22), or large posterior perisylvian lesions, cause it. The traditional attribution to the arcuate fasciculus is not fully supported by clinical and anatomic data.
distractors: Infarction centered in the posterior superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke area) causes the greatest impairment of auditory comprehension, which is spared here.
Broca area damage produces effortful, nonfluent speech, whereas this patient is fluent.
A left angular gyrus lesion causes alexia with agraphia and often components of Gerstmann syndrome, not a selective repetition deficit.
Lesions of the posterior left middle temporal gyrus (area 37) and angular gyrus cause transcortical sensory aphasia, in which repetition is spared but comprehension is lost.
explanation.key_point: Conduction aphasia (fluent, good comprehension, poor repetition) follows discrete supramarginal gyrus (area 40) or auditory cortex lesions.
